421 IDL constructs, twelve implementations, and the flag that aligns them

Every construct in this project's interop corpus, put through twelve independent implementations in five encodings and both byte orders: 4210 rows, 75780 cells, 35896 of them carrying octets a real serialiser really produced. The page answers three questions in this order — whether any of the other eleven encodes something this one cannot, which setting makes this project's octets equal to a given peer's, and what each peer does on its own. The rows are the appendix.

If you arrived from a bug report: the row it concerns has its own address, the dialect matrix is the one-line answer to "which flag", and reported issues lists the ones already mapped onto rows.

  1. Can a peer do something we cannot?
  2. Which flag do I set?
  3. How to read a cell
  4. The twelve, one at a time
  5. Reported issues these rows answer
  6. Appendix: every row

Can a peer do something we cannot?

On the wire, no. Of the 421 constructs measured, 1 are encoded by one of the other eleven implementations and refused by this one. This project encodes 417 of 421. The 3 nothing encodes — primitive-char-above-latin1 and primitive-wchar-above-bmp and recursive-array — are refused by all twelve alike, because the OMG IDL-to-C++ and IDL-to-Java mappings give char and wchar no room for the value the case carries.

That is the answer for the corpus, and the corpus is a corpus of data types: things that can be declared, filled with a value and put on a wire. The question has a second half — what each project's IDL compiler will accept at all — and there the answer is not the same one. Both halves are below.

What each system took, and what it turned away

A construct is taken by a system when that system produced octets for it in at least one encoding and byte order. The last two columns are the question above, asked per system. A system that could not be asked at all — no encoding version 2, one byte order, no form for the construct in its type model — is not refusing anything, and those rows are counted apart in its own section.

Which half of the language each compiler accepts

OMG IDL 4.2 is not one language. §7.4 divides it into fifteen building blocks, rules (1) to (227), and §9 names the profiles — sets of blocks — that middleware is written against. Most implementations pick a profile. This project takes all fifteen, so the column that matters is the last one: the rules it does not take yet, each of which is an item on a list rather than a boundary.

A drop is a third verdict and not a soft yes: the compiler exits 0, prints that it discarded the construct, and generates code without it. Whether a construct a compiler accepted silently also survives to its output is a separate measurement — and it is the one the rest of this page makes.

Which flag do I set?

Implementations disagree about questions the specification leaves open, and about a few it does not. Rather than pick one reading and call the rest wrong, this project carries every measured reading as a setting. A dialect is a named bundle of those decisions — one per implementation whose octets were measured — and three further flags cover readings no dialect holds.

How to read one line of it

Take a column: a peer. The figure under its name is how many rows that peer produced octets for at all — never 3,350, because no peer was asked every row. A peer with no encoding version 2 was not asked three of the five encodings; one that writes a single byte order was not asked the other; a construct its type model has no form for was never put to it. None of that is disagreement, so none of it is in these numbers.

Take a cell: how many of that peer's rows this project does not reproduce under that setting — the rows where the peer wrote octets and this project, under that flag, wrote different ones. Lower is better and zero is byte-for-byte everywhere. The cell shows what is left over rather than what is covered, because the leftover is the finding: 62 rows where RTI and this project write different octets under RTI's own dialect is a list of work, and "806 covered" is the same fact with the work hidden behind a subtraction. Every cell is a link into the rows it counts, and each peer's leftover is broken down by cause in its own section.

What each setting decides

--dialect specification
A clause-by-clause reading of XTypes 1.3, which is what the text says rather than what any product does — and what this project ships. An unannotated aggregate is @appendable (§7.3.1.2.1.8), collection delimiters follow rules 9 and 12, a member's must-understand bit is written as declared and on every @key member, a wstring's code units go out in the stream's byte order, and a negative case label of a narrow signed discriminator selects its branch. No measured implementation produces it in full, which is the cost of the default rather than an argument against it: a peer's number in this row is how much of what that peer writes the text also writes.
--dialect cyclone
Eclipse Cyclone DDS 11.0.1 — a dialect like the other eight, and no longer the default. An aggregate whose IDL carried no extensibility annotation is taken to be @final, so it gains no delimiter header under encoding version 2; a @mutable member under version 1 always takes the extended parameter header; an EMHEADER takes the compact length code; a wstring's code units go out in the host's byte order; a negative case label of a signed discriminator narrower than 32 bits selects no branch at all. The last two are why the default moved.
--dialect rti
RTI Connext DDS 7.7. An unannotated aggregate is @appendable, so it gains a four-octet delimiter header under encoding version 2; no collection carries a delimiter of its own; a @mutable member's EMHEADER reuses the nested delimiter as its length rather than writing one.
--dialect fastdds
eProsima Fast DDS with Fast CDR 2.3.5. An unannotated aggregate is @appendable; an enumeration counts as a primitive when deciding whether a collection is delimited; an EMHEADER takes the short length code wherever the length fits in it; a member's must-understand bit is left off the wire.
--dialect omniorb
omniORB 4.3.3 over CORBA CDR, which is encoding version 1 — CORBA 3.3 part 2 §9.3. A two-octet transmission code set, GIOP 1.2's length-prefixed wchar, and a byte-order mark inside every wstring.
--dialect tao
TAO 2.5.24 over CORBA CDR. A four-octet transmission code set and GIOP 1.2's length-prefixed wchar, which together make its wstring the one form no DDS implementation writes: an octet count over wide units.
--dialect jacorb
JacORB 3.9 over CORBA CDR. A two-octet code set like omniORB's and GIOP 1.2's wchar, with no byte-order mark: it reads the units big-endian whatever the stream says.
--dialect opendds
OpenDDS 3.34.0 over OpenDDS::DCPS::Serializer. Fast DDS's XCDR1 @mutable framing with a parameter id no other implementation writes — PID_IMPL_EXTENSION and PID_MUST_UNDERSTAND set on every member whatever the member declared — an XCDR2 length code that is short where the serialised length fits and never reuses a nested delimiter, @key implying must-understand as §7.2.2.4.4.4.8 requires, and a front end that carries neither @value nor @bit_bound as far as a serialiser.
--dialect ros-fastrtps
rosidl_typesupport_fastrtps_c 2.2.2, ROS 2 Humble — not Fast DDS: it generates its own serialisation. Encoding version 1 only, every message @final whatever its .idl says, a wstring counted in characters over four-octet code units whose octets stay in the host's order while the length swaps, and a four-octet scalar wchar that does swap.
--dialect ros-cyclone
rmw_cyclonedds_cpp 1.3.4, ROS 2 Humble — not Cyclone: it walks the introspection type support. The same wstring cell as ros-fastrtps over units in the stream's order, and a two-octet scalar wchar beside those four-octet units, which is the one place in the nine where the two widths part. It writes the host's byte order and takes no argument for it, so half its column does not exist.
--length-codes universal-nextint
One question, changed on its own: every @mutable member's EMHEADER carries an explicit four-octet length whatever the member's size or shape. Four octets more per member than any dialect writes, and no measured implementation writes it — reach for it against a peer that expects that form, or to reproduce a recorded capture octet for octet.
--map-length rule-15-omits
One question, changed on its own: a delimited map omits its entry count, which is rule (15) read as written and is what OpenDDS's generated code does — its operator<< writes the delimiter under version 2 and the count under version 1, as alternatives rather than as both.

A dialect is a writer-side and a reader-side setting at once: --dialect rti means "write what RTI writes" exactly as it means "read what RTI writes". Setting one to reach a peer therefore changes what every other peer sees, which is why the table has twelve columns and not one. The row marked how it should be is not a peer: it is the clause-by-clause reading of XTypes 1.3, and its column tells you how far each implementation is from the text. It is also the shipped default — what this project writes when nobody names a dialect is what the text says, not what any product does — so the same row carries both tags.

How to read a cell

The mode: plain-cdr1/le and its nine siblings

Every construct is measured ten times, and the mode says which of the ten a row is. It is two things joined by a slash. Before the slash is the encoding: how the type's members are framed on the wire — whether there is a length in front of the aggregate, whether each member carries its own id. After it is the byte order the numbers inside are written in: le is little-endian, what an x86 or an ARM writes natively, and be is big-endian, which the CDR standard calls the default and which a PowerPC or a SPARC writes. Neither is more correct; a stream declares which one it used, and a reader that ignores the declaration reads every number backwards.

encodingversionwhat it frames
plain-cdr1XCDR1The classic CDR of CORBA and of DDS before XTypes: the members in declaration order, each aligned to its own size, and nothing else. No length prefix, no member ids. A reader must already know the type exactly.
pl-cdr1XCDR1Parameter-list CDR, version 1: each member preceded by its id and its length, so a reader can step over a member it does not know. This is what a @mutable type takes under encoding version 1.
plain-cdr2XCDR2XTypes' version 2 of the plain form. The same idea as plain-cdr1 with different alignment rules — an eight-octet member aligns to four, not to eight — which is why the two are not the same octets for the same type.
delimited-cdrXCDR2Version 2 with a delimiter header: a four-octet length in front of the aggregate, so a reader that meets members it does not know can jump the rest. This is what an @appendable type takes, and it is at the centre of most cross-vendor surprises, because whether a type is appendable is exactly what implementations disagree about.
pl-cdr2XCDR2Version 2's parameter list: a delimiter, then every member behind an EMHEADER carrying its id, its length code and its must-understand bit. The framing of a @mutable type under version 2.

A type does not pick its framing directly. Its extensibility does — @final, @appendable or @mutable — and the encoding version picks between the two versions of that framing. That is why a foreign column answers five encodings with two runs: its command line takes the version, and the framing follows from the type. Those rows read = plain-cdr1 or = plain-cdr2 and link to the run they are.

The words a cell can carry

12B, 48B, a number and a B
The system ran, took the type, took the value, and produced that many octets. The cell links to the file holding exactly those octets, and opening a row shows them in full.
same
In the read direction: it read its own bytes back and got the value the case says it should. This is the only outcome that demonstrates a round trip rather than an encoding.
different
It read its own bytes back and got something else. Wherever this appears it is a defect, in whichever implementation it appears in, because nothing but that implementation wrote those bytes.
refused
It ran and would not take the type or the value, and the cell links to the sentence it gave. A refusal is a result: it is the compiler or the serialiser naming a construct it does not have.
unwritten
There was nothing to read, because the write direction produced nothing. It says nothing whatever about the reader, and it is printed rather than left blank so that it cannot be mistaken for agreement.
= plain-cdr1
This row's run is that row's run. A foreign command line selects the encoding version and not the framing, so four of the five encodings point at the two runs the system actually made rather than at five identical files.
no xcdr2
The system has no encoding version 2 at all. CORBA CDR predates XTypes and Fast CDR 1.0.24 has none, so three of the five encodings were never a question that could be put to it.
one order
The system writes one byte order and this row is the other one. TAO writes little endian only because ACE_OutputCDR swaps only in a build configuration this one did not use; JacORB writes big endian only because its output stream has no method to set the other.
no form
The construct has no form in this system's type model, so its compiler never saw the case. Nothing was asked, so nothing was refused, and the two are counted apart everywhere on this page.
no probe
The toolchain exists and no probe in this tree drives it for this slot.
not measured
The construct is expressible, a harness in this tree produces it, and no run is recorded. The cell names the command that would produce one.
w1, w2, …
Its compiler said something about the type while accepting it — that many distinct warnings, linked. A marker of its own rather than a note beside a refusal, because the row it matters most in is the one where nothing went wrong: a system whose bytes agree while its compiler warned about the type is not the same as one that agreed silently.

Following a cell to the real output

A cell that carries octets links to the file holding them, byte for byte, as <construct>/<system>/<encoding>.<order>.bin; every other cell links to the STATUS file carrying that system's own sentence about the slot; a warning marker links to what its compiler printed. The links are relative to the directory this page sits in, which is the result tree itself, so they resolve from a checkout on disk and from anywhere the directory is served whole. As this page was built the tree is not part of the public mirror at github.com/zero-objects/zero-dds, so no absolute link is emitted: a link into a tree that is not published is a link to a 404, and a reader who follows one has been told something false about the evidence. Regenerating with --base-url makes every link on this page absolute the day the tree is published.

OpenDDS OpenDDS 3.34.0 / ACE 6.5.24#

The only IDL front end of the five whose map compiles, and the only DDS implementation here with CORBA/TAO lineage: opendds_idl --idl-version 4 plus tao_idl -Sa -St produces the classic C++ mapping, so wireprobe-opendds takes the same CORBA C++ fill the omniORB and TAO probes take. OpenDDS::DCPS::Serializer, whose Encoding carries both the version and the byte order, so one build answers all four combinations. Its 504 refusals are the CORBA C++ fill's and are worded as the probe's, not the vendor's: OpenDDS's own front end parses map, and wireprobe-fill's CORBA C++ output has no form for one.

HDDS HDDS, hddsgen 1.2.0#

The second pure-Rust DDS implementation. hddsgen gen rust generates the type and its own encode_* methods; wireprobe-hdds compiles that output unedited against the declaration shim in tools/wireprobe/hdds-shim/, because the published hdds crate does not carry the trait surface the generated code implements. Structural limits, each measured: no big-endian encoder, no parameter-list encoder — one framing per encoding version, whatever the type's extensibility says — and a front end that accepts all corpus cases it parses while its serialiser frames @appendable and @mutable types as @final, with no DHEADER and no EMHEADER. Dialect::Hdds carries those departures, opt-in, and reproduces every recorded row.

OpenSplice OpenSplice Community Edition 6.9 (OSPL_V6_9_210323OSS_RELEASE)#

idlpp -S -l cpp (standalone C++, the CORBA C++ mapping) plus DDS::OpenSplice::CdrTypeSupport::serialize. Its IDL is OMG IDL 3.5: no annotation parses, keys are #pragma keylist, so wireprobe-opensplice rewrites a case only where every construct means the same XCDR1 bytes in that IDL and refuses the rest by name — @mutable, @optional, @external, @must_understand, @value, an enum @bit_bound below 32, bitmask, bitset, map, and a union as the topic type. idlpp itself refuses wchar, wstring, fixed, struct inheritance, empty structs, octet and int8/uint8 discriminators and struct-typed key members. Four cases are accepted by idlpp and its own generated C++ does not compile: the three recursive types (forward-declared structs are defined twice), a type named static, and an unsigned long long case label above the signed range.

JacORB JacORB 3.9#

org.jacorb.idl.parser plus CDROutputStream. Writes big endian only: org.jacorb.orb.CDROutputStream has no setLittleEndian — only CDRInputStream does. It refuses 24 cases, which is the most of the three, and 14 of them are two defects of its own rather than J9's discriminator question. A union case label outside the signed range of its Java holder: Illegal case label <3735928559> for integral switch type int for an unsigned long discriminator, the same for unsigned long long, long long treated as 32-bit, and unsigned short reaching javac as Choice.java:33: error: incompatible types: possible lossy conversion from int to short in JacORB's own generated code — eight cases. A default: branch it can only give discriminator 0: the generated fraction(int _discriminator, double _x) throws BAD_OPERATION for any other, so a sample selecting the default with an unlisted label has no JacORB form — six cases, array-1d-union, sequence-union and union-with-default.

A construct built from a bug report names the report in its own README, and every construct whose compiler draws the same diagnostic has the same cause — so a reporter who lands on any of them gets the same answer. The numbers are the tracker's at github.com/zero-objects/zero-dds.

The cause behind the large family, and the two answers to it

XTypes 1.3 §7.3.1.2.1.8 lets an implementation choose what an aggregate whose source carried no extensibility annotation is taken to be, and nothing on the wire says which choice was made. Cyclone chooses @final and says so in a compiler warning it prints on every such type. RTI and Fast DDS choose @appendable, which under encoding version 2 puts a four-octet delimiter header in front of the aggregate that the other side is not expecting — so the reader takes the first four octets of the payload for a length and everything after it is wrong. Under encoding version 1 the two readings are byte for byte identical, which is why the same pair of programs interoperates until somebody turns XCDR2 on, and why the symptom appears without anything in the type having changed.

There are two answers and they are not equivalent. Annotate the type. An explicit @final or @appendable in the IDL settles the question for every implementation at once, and it is the only answer that survives a third implementation joining the system. Or set the dialect of the peer you are talking to, which settles it for that peer and moves it for the rest — the matrix is the whole of what that costs.

A report can share this symptom without sharing a row. #27 reaches the same framing question through a different reported failure, and the rows here answer only the framing half of it; the half about whether two participants find each other at all is not a question about octets and is not measured on this page. A report is listed above only when a construct in the corpus was built from it or draws the same diagnostic.

Appendix: every row

4210 rows: 421 constructs × five encodings × two byte orders. Search by anything a row carries — a construct name, a mode, an issue number, a sentence a compiler printed — or by the symptom, which is what a bug report gives you. Every term you type has to appear, and every row has its own address, so a row is something you can paste into a reply.

Asking about one system. A system and a symptom join with a colon: cyclone:differs is every row where Cyclone's octets are not ours, rti:refused every row RTI would not take, fastdds:misread every row Fast DDS read back wrongly, and opendds:warned every row its compiler said something about. The names are cyclone, rti, fastdds, opendds, hdds, opensplice, omniorb, tao, jacorb, ros-fastrtps, ros-cyclone, zerodds-rust, zerodds-c, zerodds-cpp, zerodds-csharp, zerodds-java, zerodds-python, zerodds-typescript. On their own, differs, refused, misread, warned and unalignable ask the same questions of every system at once.
